research_theme: Robustness to noisy and counterfactual retrieved context
research_question: How do retrieval quality and misleading context affect RAG outputs?
focal_claim_text: For counterfactual robustness, ChatGPT-English accuracy fell from 89% without documents to 9% with counterfactual documents, with a reported error-correction rate of 57.14%.
comparison_claim_text: As corpus size increases to approximately 3,000 documents, MRR@3 falls below 0.5 for the evaluated retrieval settings.
adjudication_rationale: The two papers expose different ways that retrieved context can undermine a RAG system. RGB tests whether a generator can resist misleading counterfactual documents: for ChatGPT-English, accuracy falls from 89% without documents to 9% with counterfactual documents, with a reported error-correction rate of 57.14%. T2-RAGBench examines retrieval as the corpus grows and reports that MRR@3 drops below 50% at around 3,000 documents for the evaluated settings. The first result concerns robustness after misleading evidence is supplied; the second concerns the retriever's ability to find the right document in a larger corpus. Together they contextualize two distinct failure points in a RAG pipeline, but they are not a head-to-head comparison.
source_verification: P015: PDF p.7, Table 7 (counterfactual robustness). P009: PDF p.7, §5.4 / corpus-size ablation discussion; conclusion on PDF p.8.
decision_note: Keep the mechanisms separate: counterfactual-context susceptibility is not the same as retrieval-rank degradation as corpus size increases.

research_theme: General AI scientific claim verification vs clinical transfer
research_question: Do claim-evidence verification results generalize across AI research and clinical literature?
focal_claim_text: On CLAIM-BENCH, the best reported claim-identification F1 is 0.59 (Claude 3.5), while the best evidence-extraction F1 is 0.47 (GPT-4-Turbo).
comparison_claim_text: In Oracle label prediction, the majority-voting ensemble reaches macro-average F1 of 0.93 on SciFact development and 0.92 on CoVERt; the best individual-model macro-average F1 is 0.89 on both datasets.
adjudication_rationale: CLAIM-BENCH measures claim identification and evidence extraction from AI research papers. Its best reported claim-identification F1 is 0.59 (Claude 3.5), while its best evidence-extraction F1 is 0.47 (GPT-4-Turbo). CliVER's cited result is Oracle-setting support/refute/neutral label prediction on SciFact and CoVERt, where majority voting reaches macro-F1 0.93 and 0.92 respectively. These are different pipeline stages: extracting claim/evidence spans is not the same task as classifying a claim-evidence pair after relevant evidence is supplied. CliVER is also clinical/biomedical transfer evidence. The scores cannot be compared as if they measured one common benchmark capability.
source_verification: P008: PDF p.7, Table 2. P021: PDF p.5, Table 3 and accompanying Oracle-setting label-prediction results.
decision_note: Do not rank 0.59/0.47 extraction F1 against 0.93/0.92 Oracle label macro-F1; task and evaluation conditions differ.

research_theme: General AI scientific claim verification vs clinical transfer
research_question: Do claim-evidence verification results generalize across AI research and clinical literature?
focal_claim_text: On CLAIM-BENCH, the best reported claim-identification F1 is 0.59 (Claude 3.5), while the best evidence-extraction F1 is 0.47 (GPT-4-Turbo).
comparison_claim_text: In the Open clinician-review setting, the reported agreement/accuracy was 79.0% for abstract retrieval, 67.4% for sentence selection, and 63.2% for label prediction.
adjudication_rationale: CLAIM-BENCH reports automated claim-identification and evidence-extraction F1 against sentence-level annotations on AI papers. CliVER's Open clinician-review percentages measure three separate stages in a clinical verification pipeline: abstract retrieval relevance (79.0%), sentence-selection relevance (67.4%), and label agreement (63.2%). These are human-rated stage-level accuracies/relevance judgments, not extraction F1 scores, and they arise from a different domain and sample. The results may both reveal difficulty in evidence-grounded systems, but they are not directly comparable.
source_verification: P008: PDF p.7, Table 2. P021: PDF pp.6–7, Open-setting clinician review for abstract retrieval, sentence selection and label prediction.
decision_note: Do not call all CliVER percentages 'agreement': 79.0% and 67.4% are relevance/accuracy assessments; 63.2% is label agreement.

research_theme: General AI scientific claim verification vs clinical transfer
research_question: Do claim-evidence verification results generalize across AI research and clinical literature?
focal_claim_text: On CLAIM-BENCH, the best reported claim-identification F1 is 0.59 (Claude 3.5), while the best evidence-extraction F1 is 0.47 (GPT-4-Turbo).
comparison_claim_text: CliVER's real-world clinician evaluation used 19 clinical research claims from six disease categories and did not measure retrieval recall because exhaustive review of all relevant PubMed abstracts was not feasible.
adjudication_rationale: CLAIM-BENCH evaluates claim and evidence extraction on a validation subset drawn from AI research papers. CliVER's real-world clinician evaluation used 19 clinical research claims across six disease categories and explicitly did not measure retrieval recall because exhaustive review of all relevant PubMed abstracts was infeasible. This adds useful context about a practical limitation in evaluating end-to-end scientific claim verification: a system may be assessed on the relevance of retrieved items without having a complete recall denominator. However, CliVER's clinical setting and evaluation design do not directly test CLAIM-BENCH or establish its recall. The two findings should be linked as complementary evaluation limitations, not compared as model performance.
source_verification: P008: PDF pp.7–8, Table 2 and evaluation discussion. P021: PDF p.1 abstract and PDF p.5 evaluation design; recall limitation is stated explicitly.
decision_note: The 19-claim clinical evaluation is a small real-world review and does not provide exhaustive retrieval recall. Do not infer that CLAIM-BENCH has the same limitation without checking its own protocol.

research_theme: Inter-annotator agreement across evidence annotation tasks
research_question: Are annotation reliability problems comparable across scientific evidence extraction and factuality annotation?
focal_claim_text: Inter-annotator agreement is substantially lower for evidence annotation (κ=0.30) than for claim annotation (κ=0.66) on the 30-paper validation subset.
comparison_claim_text: Human annotator agreement was fair/low for scientific check-worthiness (κ=.29, 77% raw) and factuality (κ=.30, 72% raw) in the pilot study.
adjudication_rationale: Both studies report weaker agreement when annotators must make evidence-related or factuality judgments, but the annotation tasks are not identical. CLAIM-BENCH reports Cohen's κ=.66 for claim identification and κ=.30 for evidence identification on a 30-paper subset; its evidence labels require locating dispersed supporting sentences, where boundary differences and multiple valid spans can reduce agreement. SCIFACTCHECK reports κ=.29 for scientific check-worthiness and κ=.30 for factuality, with raw agreement of 77% and 72% respectively. The similar κ values are informative context that annotation reliability is a challenge across scientific evaluation tasks, but they should not be treated as a direct replication or pooled estimate because the constructs, annotation units and protocols differ.
source_verification: P008: PDF p.18, Appendix B.3 (30-paper subset; κ=.66 claims, κ=.30 evidence). P010: PDF p.7, §6.1 (check-worthiness κ=.29, factuality κ=.30; raw agreement 77% and 72%).
decision_note: Numerically similar kappa values do not prove equivalent annotation difficulty. Keep claim identification, evidence identification, check-worthiness and factuality as separate constructs.
